written: 2026-09-10 (v1); v2 the same day, after the test that enforces it was found to be reading two files out of eight
why_this_file_exists: The pre-paper's first rule reads 'five states, no sixth', as though one vocabulary governed everything this record holds. There are two, they share the field name 'state', and they meet in the published snapshot where a reader cannot tell them apart. Neither was written down anywhere, so neither could be asserted and a new value in either would have been nobody's decision. Both are written here so that adding a state is a deliberate act with a reason, and research/test_states.py fails if one appears that is not. v2: four values were in the record and not in this file - `derived`, `nothing_to_do`, `paused` and `failed` - because the test enforcing it listed one directory level while the record nests, and because one of the four was permitted by an exception written into the test rather than by a declaration written here. A vocabulary enforced by a test that cannot see the record is not enforced.

epistemic.what_it_is: What this record knows about a MEASUREMENT: how its time is known, and whether there is a value at all. This is the vocabulary the pre-paper's rule 1 is about, and the only one a reader of a number needs.
epistemic.where_it_lives: It is NOT a field on a row. A row in data/live/rows carries no 'state' at all: the epistemic state is derived from phenomenonTime, phenomenonTimeUnknown, phenomenonTimeCorrected, resultQuality and whether result is null. The state is computed where the value is rendered, which is why a row cannot carry a wrong one.

states.observed: the source published a measurement time and we take it as served
states.untimed: we know the value and when it reached us, never when it was true, because the source publishes no measurement time
states.estimated: a value or a time this record computed rather than received - including our correction of a source's clock, which is our reading and never the source's statement
states.forecast: a value about a time that has not happened
states.unavailable: there is no value. A state, not a blank, and never a zero

epistemic.no_sixth: A sixth would mean this record can know something about a measurement in a way it has not described. If one is ever needed, it is added here first, with a sentence saying what a reader is to understand by it.

pipeline.what_it_is: What HAPPENED to a derived row on its way through an organ. It says nothing about the world and nothing about how well anything is known; it is the record of a process. It is a field on the row because it is a fact about that row.
pipeline.where_it_lives: data/live/derived/*/**.jsonl - including the nested ones: the notebook of each entity and the voice benchmarks - and the receipts beside them, and it travels into public/live-snapshot.json under the same key name as the epistemic state, which is the ambiguity this file names and does not yet fix. The nesting is stated here because the first test written to enforce this file listed one level and saw two files out of eight, and the only file carrying an undeclared value was among the six it never opened.

states.rejected: an utterance the validator refused, kept with its reason
states.retracted: an utterance withdrawn after it was made
states.organelle: an intermediate step in a conversation, not an utterance about the city
states.claim_settled: a prediction reached its due time and was scored
states.voiced: a Serbian rendering that passed its own validation
states.refused: a Serbian rendering the validator refused, kept with its text since C-033
states.organ_silent: the model daemon did not answer
states.organ_failed: the call raised, and the receipt carries the exception
states.estimated: the news organ's own classification of a headline - the ONE value that appears in both vocabularies, and it is the epistemic one: a category this record computed rather than received
states.derived: an organ tick that produced something. It is written on the TICK RECEIPT rather than on a row, and it travels into the published snapshot, where it was being allowed by a hard-coded exception in the test instead of being declared here.
states.nothing_to_do: an organ tick that found nothing to work on. Not a fault and not a silence: there was no work, and the receipt says so rather than saying nothing.
states.incomplete: the model omitted a headline or a required classification field; retained as an incomplete attempt and never marked completed
states.waiting_retry: unfinished headlines exist but their backoff or batch limit defers this attempt
states.waiting_model: model capacity or the job deadline deferred inference before a request was sent; no classification attempt was spent
states.retry_exhausted: unfinished headlines reached the three-attempt limit; they remain visible and incomplete rather than being silently marked completed
states.reconciled: a disposable completion cache was rebuilt from retained classification records; the prior keys and reconciliation result were retained
states.paused: an organ deliberately paused by a PAUSED file. A silence somebody chose, which is why it must never read as a silence somebody failed to notice.
states.failed: the call raised - the same event `organ_failed` names, written by the voice benchmark under a shorter name. Four rows from 2026-09-09 carry it. It is DECLARED rather than corrected because a row is never edited: the record contains this value, so the vocabulary has to contain it too. New code should write `organ_failed`.

the_ambiguity_named: In public/live-snapshot.json both vocabularies appear under 'state'. A reader sees "state": "estimated" beside "state": "thought" and cannot tell that the first is a claim about knowledge and the second a note about a pipeline. This is not fixed today: renaming a published field is a change to something other people may already read, and it is worth doing deliberately rather than in the same hour it was noticed. It is written down here, and in the corrections ledger, so that it is a known defect rather than an unnoticed one.
how_to_add_a_state: Add it here with a sentence a stranger could act on, then to the code, then run the suite. In that order: the record describes what it does before it does it, or the description is a reconstruction. Never add an allowance to the test instead - an exception in a test is a declaration nobody can find.
